title: Teenagers opt in to re-teaching
statement: With adolescents, don't re-explain what a learner has shown they can do, and offer re-teaching rather than push it, since repeating what teens think they know feels infantilizing.
detail: The Grade 9 research brief, from a published review read in full, reports that middle adolescents become more alert to whether they are treated with respect and accorded high status, and that interventions repeating what teens think they already know feel infantilizing and tend to fail. It draws two rules for the lesson's guide: never re-explain something the student has already shown they can do, and make re-teaching opt-in, offered as a walkthrough, rather than pushed on every miss. The Grade 9 strategy names being talked down to as the biggest risk in porting a Grade 3 lesson.
against: The source is a review and a hypothesis built on randomized trials, not a test of reading lessons (`othello-course-renderer-draft/repo/docs/design/grade-9/research/learners-voice-guide.md`, line 15). For young learners the reading project keeps skipping instruction out of the learner's own hands, so the rule is for older learners.

evidence.quote: Interventions that repeat things teens think they already know feel infantilizing and tend to fail.
Re-teaching should be opt-in ("Want a walkthrough?"), not pushed on every miss.
Grade 9 readers punish being talked down to, and that is the biggest risk in porting a Grade 3 lesson.
